articles.title: The Supreme Court Is About to Rule on Whether Babies Born to H-1B Parents Are American Citizens
articles.excerpt: A decision expected as early as Monday could strip birthright citizenship from hundreds of thousands of children born each year to parents on temporary visas — including the quarter-million Indians on H-1B status.
articles.image_caption: The US Supreme Court building in Washington, where a ruling on birthright citizenship is expected this week
articles.nri_angle: This ruling directly affects the quarter-million Indians currently on H-1B visas in America and their families — if upheld, babies born to H-1B holders in the US would not be American citizens, potentially leaving them stateless.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: The July 31 Deadline Is Coming. Here's What Every NRI Filing an Indian Tax Return Needs to Know.
articles.excerpt: Schedule FA, the DTAA paper trail, the FBAR double bind — a practical guide to the traps that catch diaspora taxpayers every year.
articles.image_caption: Tax documents and currency on a desk during filing season
articles.nri_angle: Every NRI with Indian income faces the July 31 ITR deadline. The compliance burden is uniquely diaspora-shaped — juggling two tax systems, two sets of forms, and penalties that can reach ₹10 lakh per missed disclosure.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Fifty Years Ago, a Handful of Hare Krishnas Pulled a Chariot Down Fifth Avenue. Now 25,000 Show Up.
articles.excerpt: ISKCON's Ratha Yatra in Manhattan just marked its golden anniversary — a milestone in how the Indian diaspora practises faith in public.
articles.image_caption: Devotees pull a decorated Ratha Yatra chariot at an ISKCON festival in the United States
articles.nri_angle: The Ratha Yatra is the diaspora's most visible public expression of Hindu devotion in the West. For Indian-American families, ISKCON centres have become anchors of cultural continuity — the neighbourhood temple transplanted to Brooklyn and Trafalgar Square.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Modi Wrote in Creole to a Diaspora That Has Been in Seychelles Since Before America Was a Country
articles.excerpt: India's prime minister is visiting a 115-island archipelago in the Indian Ocean where Tamil settlers arrived in 1770 — and where Indians now make up nearly a tenth of the population.
articles.image_caption: The clock tower in Victoria, Mahé — the capital of Seychelles and the smallest capital city in the world
articles.nri_angle: The Indian community in Seychelles is one of the oldest continuous diaspora settlements in the world, yet remains almost invisible to the broader NRI conversation. Modi's visit — and his choice to address them in the local Creole language — underscores how far-flung India's people-to-people ties really are, even in a nation of just 121,000.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Saudi Arabia Just Told 2.4 Million Indians They Can Stop Renting. Few Know What That Actually Means.
articles.excerpt: A new digital portal lets foreigners buy property across the Kingdom for the first time — opening the door for millions of Indian workers who have spent decades as tenants in the Gulf's biggest economy.
articles.image_caption: The Riyadh skyline — Saudi Arabia's capital and the centre of its expanding real estate market
articles.nri_angle: For the 2.4 million Indians living in Saudi Arabia — the largest expatriate group in the Kingdom — the ability to own property transforms the economic equation of Gulf migration from temporary labor to potential long-term investment and stability.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Haldiram's at Leicester Square, Drāvida in the East Village: Indian Restaurants Are Finally Playing Offence Abroad
articles.excerpt: An 88-year-old snack empire, a Food Network champion, and two Goa-to-London restaurateurs are betting that the diaspora's food has been undersold for too long.
articles.nri_angle: These openings reflect the diaspora's long frustration that the food they actually grew up eating — regional, street-level, migration-shaped — rarely made it onto restaurant menus abroad. The new wave is correcting that.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: The Son of Indian and Ukrainian Immigrants Is About to Board the ISS. He Brought His Stethoscope.
articles.excerpt: NASA astronaut Anil Menon, SpaceX's first flight surgeon and a US Space Force colonel, launches for an eight-month station mission on July 14 — adding a new chapter to the diaspora's quietly growing presence in orbit.
articles.image_caption: NASA astronaut Anil Menon in his official flight suit portrait at Johnson Space Center
articles.nri_angle: Menon, born to Indian and Ukrainian immigrant parents in Minneapolis, represents the diaspora's expanding footprint beyond corporate boardrooms and into one of the last frontiers. His mission builds on the legacy of Kalpana Chawla, Sunita Williams, and Raja Chari.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Paris Is About to Get Europe's First Traditional Hindu Temple. Thousands of Diaspora Devotees Are Already Packing.
articles.excerpt: BAPS Swaminarayan Hindu Mandir opens in September with a 13-day Festival of Culture — boat processions on the Seine, Vedic rituals, and a Parisian exhibition that places the temple alongside Notre-Dame.
articles.image_caption: Swaminarayan Akshardham in Delhi, built in the same tradition as the upcoming BAPS mandir in Paris
articles.nri_angle: The Paris mandir crystallises a pattern the diaspora has been pursuing for two decades: building permanent, architecturally ambitious Hindu sacred spaces abroad — from Robbinsville to Abu Dhabi — that anchor community identity for generations. For NRIs across Europe, it means no longer flying to London or India for a traditional temple experience.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: The Diaspora Built an American Dream. It Forgot to Plan for Getting Old in It.
articles.excerpt: A Queens nonprofit is building robotised food pantries and affordable housing for South Asian seniors. A California volunteer group charges five dollars a class. Across the country, the infrastructure to age with dignity in a foreign land is being improvised from scratch.
articles.image_caption: An elderly woman participating in a community yoga session
articles.nri_angle: The first large wave of Indian professionals arrived in America after the 1965 Immigration Act. Sixty years later, that cohort is entering its seventies and eighties — in a country whose elder-care infrastructure was not designed for people who speak Gujarati, eat vegetarian, and expect their children to live under the same roof. The story of how the community is scrambling to fill the gap is a defining NRI challenge of this decade.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: America's Oldest Indian Association Just Honoured Seven of Its Own. Four Were Doctors.
articles.excerpt: The AIA-NY benefit gala in Flushing celebrated a community's elite — and quietly revealed how narrow the diaspora's definition of success still is, even as a new generation pushes at the edges.
articles.image_caption: A Bharatanatyam dancer performs a classical Indian dance on stage, the kind of cultural showcase that anchors diaspora community galas.
articles.nri_angle: The honours list of the oldest national Indian-American association is a ritual of self-definition for a community built on professional-visa migration — and a window into whether its founding-era institutions can hold the loyalty of a startup-minded next generation.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Australia Just Honoured Ten Indian-Origin Citizens. None of Them Are Famous.
articles.excerpt: The 2026 King's Birthday Honours List reads like a map of how a migrant community embeds itself — through doctors, psychiatrists and the half-century grind of building institutions nobody else would.
articles.image_caption: Sydney's skyline, including the Opera House. Indians are now Australia's second-largest migrant community.
articles.nri_angle: Honours conferred by the Australian state — not by an Indian-community body — are a signal of belonging, recognising decades of professional and civic service by a migrant population that is now the country's second-largest.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Delhi Spent Years Wanting the Diaspora's Remittances. Now It Wants Its Portfolio.
articles.excerpt: A new RBI deposit scheme and the rise of GIFT City are reframing overseas Indians from senders of money home into investors in India — on terms built to compete with Dubai and New York.
articles.image_caption: Gujarat International Finance Tec-City (GIFT City), India's tax-neutral financial hub courting NRI capital
articles.nri_angle: Overseas Indians are being courted with hedged, leveraged double-digit returns and tax-efficient GIFT City products that let them treat India as a serious portfolio allocation rather than just a place to send remittances.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Forbes Named America's 250 Most Successful Immigrants. Twenty-Six Are Indian.
articles.excerpt: Timed to the US's 250th anniversary, the list reads like a diaspora scoreboard — and quietly maps both how far Indian-Americans have climbed and where they still haven't.
articles.image_caption: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, one of 26 Indian-origin leaders on the inaugural Forbes 250 immigrants list
articles.nri_angle: The Forbes immigrant list is a measure of how thoroughly the Indian diaspora has woven itself into the top of the American economy — and an instruction, for a community fond of measuring itself, on the boardrooms and offices it still hasn't cracked.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: The Quiet Clause in the India-UK Trade Deal That Puts Money Back in Diaspora Payslips
articles.excerpt: From 15 July, a Double Contribution Convention ends the double social-security charge on Indian professionals posted to Britain — the human core of a deal usually sold on tariffs.
articles.image_caption: Indian Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal, in London for talks ahead of the India-UK trade pact rollout
articles.nri_angle: For the thousands of Indian professionals rotated through British client sites, the Double Contribution Convention ends years of paying into a UK pension they would never collect — a small, specific win for the diaspora inside a sweeping trade pact.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk
